result: The study collected blood samples from 121 donors without known blood disorders, most with self-reported African ancestry, plus one hereditary elliptocytosis (HE) patient as a positive control. Whole-exome sequencing and principal component analysis confirmed that donors fell along a continuum from African to European ancestry, with all donors unrelated except for one six-member family.
evaluation: Claims C21-C27 describe the study cohort and genetic characterization. The methodology is clearly stated with appropriate controls (HE patient), and the PCA analysis (Figure 1A) and kinship coefficients provide robust evidence for the population structure claims. Sample size and design are appropriate for the study objectives.

result: Among healthy donors, 16% carried pathogenic hemoglobin alleles (5 HbAS, 4 HbAC, 11 α-thalassemia), and 32% carried G6PD polymorphisms associated with deficiency. No alleles for β-thalassemia or xerocytosis were detected. The remaining 68 unrelated donors were classified as 'non-carriers' of known disease alleles.
evaluation: Claims C28-C37 report genetic screening results with specific counts and classifications. The findings are supported by exome sequencing data (Figure 1B) and appropriate genotyping methods (including PCR for PIEZO1 E756del and coverage analysis for HBA2 deletions). The classification scheme is clearly defined and appropriate for subsequent analyses.

result: P. falciparum growth rates among non-carriers showed a threefold range (64-136% for 3D7, 76-128% for Th.026.09) that was strongly correlated between strains (R²=0.69, p<3×10⁻¹⁶) and reproducible across weeks. Known disease alleles (α-thalassemia, HbAS, HE) reduced growth as expected, but the non-carrier distribution substantially overlapped with carriers, implying previously unknown RBC variation impacts parasite growth with cumulative effects comparable to known disease alleles.
evaluation: Claims C38-C47 present core experimental findings on parasite growth variation. The data are supported by rigorous batch correction methods (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), biological replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and statistical analyses showing strong strain correlation and expected effects of disease alleles. The inference about unknown variation (C47) is well-justified by the observed overlap between non-carrier and carrier distributions.

result: P. falciparum invasion rates among non-carriers ranged from 70-143% for 3D7 and 41-193% for Th.026.09, with weaker strain correlation (R²=0.10) than growth. HbAC reduced 3D7 invasion by 11% (p=0.008), while α-thalassemia increased Th.026.09 invasion by 22% (p=0.091). Greater batch effects and variability suggest invasion is influenced by greater experimental noise than growth.
evaluation: Claims C48-C55 report invasion data with appropriate statistical support. The authors acknowledge greater experimental noise (Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2) and weaker correlations, which is consistent with the technical challenges of measuring invasion. The inference about experimental noise (C55) is well-supported by the batch effect and reproducibility analyses. Missing invasion data for 10 non-carriers is noted in methods.

result: RBC phenotypes from complete blood counts, osmotic fragility tests, and ektacytometry showed that disease alleles were associated with characteristic abnormalities (HbAC with dehydration, α-thalassemia with microcytic anemia, HE with extreme fragility and non-deformability). However, broad distributions in non-carriers overlapped most carrier distributions for all phenotypic measures, with variation ranges (e.g., 24 fl for MCV) large compared to African-European differences (3-5 fl), suggesting healthy RBCs exist on the same phenotypic continuum as disease-carrying RBCs.
evaluation: Claims C56-C65 describe comprehensive RBC phenotyping with appropriate statistical comparisons (t-tests, p<0.1 threshold justified by sample size). The data are presented in Figure 3 and supplements with clear visualization of distributions. The inference about a phenotypic continuum (C61, C65) is well-supported by the observed overlap and is consistent with polygenic trait architecture. The comparison to African-European differences (C60) provides important context.

result: Among 25 tested RBC phenotypes, Ohyper (tendency to retain deformability when dehydrated) was most strongly predictive of P. falciparum fitness in non-carriers. RBCs with largest Ohyper values supported 22-46% faster growth and 31-83% more effective invasion than those with smallest values. Parasites also grew faster in RBCs with larger volume (MCV), greater hemoglobin mass (MCH), and more deformable membranes (DImax), while baseline dehydration (higher CHCM) inhibited replication.
evaluation: Claims C66-C74 report univariate associations between RBC phenotypes and parasite fitness with appropriate statistical tests (OLS regression, p-values reported). The findings are biologically coherent and consistent with prior experimental manipulations (cited). However, these are univariate associations selected from LASSO models, so the p-values should be interpreted cautiously. The overall conclusion (C74) is well-supported by the pattern of associations.

result: LASSO models using non-carrier phenotypes explained 3-9% of variation in parasite growth in test data (significantly greater than permutations), but did not explain invasion variation better than chance. Models were less predictive for clinical isolate Th.026.09 than lab strain 3D7. Prediction error was greater for extreme values. Non-carrier cells less hospitable to parasites share traits with disease-carrying RBCs: smaller size, decreased deformability, and increased tendency to lose deformability when dehydrating.
evaluation: Claims C75-C80 report LASSO cross-validation results with appropriate permutation controls (Figure 4B-C). The modest R² values (3-9%) are realistic for complex traits and significantly exceed permutation expectations. The failure to predict invasion (C78) is consistent with the greater experimental noise documented earlier. The summary inference (C80) appropriately synthesizes the phenotypic associations. The k-folds CV approach with 10,000 iterations provides robust validation.

result: LASSO models combining genotypes and phenotypes from 23 malaria-related genes explained 7-15% of variation in parasite growth (significantly more than permutations and random gene sets), suggesting these genes contain variation influencing P. falciparum development. Thirty-two polymorphisms were selected, occurring in ion channels (PIEZO1 with 7 variants, ATP2B4), membrane backbone proteins (SPTA1, SPTB, ANK1, SLC4A1, EPB42), and plasma membrane proteins/invasion receptors (ABCB6, GYPB, GYPC, CR1, CD44, BSG). PIEZO1-E756del predicted 7.9% reduction in Th.026.09 growth but was not related to dehydration. An ATP2B4 variant previously implicated by GWAS was functionally associated with P. falciparum fitness for the first time.
evaluation: Claims C81-C96 report genetic associations using a hypothesis-driven approach focused on 23 candidate genes. The LASSO CV framework with permutation and random gene set controls (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) provides strong evidence that these genes are enriched for functional variants. The specific variants identified (Figure 5A) are biologically plausible, with many in genes previously linked to malaria or RBC function. The ATP2B4 finding (C88-C90) is particularly notable as the first functional demonstration. The approach is appropriately powered for candidate gene analysis but not for genome-wide discovery (acknowledged in C132).

result: Among the 32 LASSO-selected variants, 18 were synonymous (not significantly different from input proportion, p=0.72). Over half have been previously associated with gene expression, GWAS traits, or GWAS loci through linkage, suggesting they tag functional polymorphisms. Novel variants contribute substantially to model predictive power, and nearly all variants are novel in terms of association with P. falciparum growth rate.
evaluation: Claims C97-C100 characterize the selected variants with appropriate statistical tests (binomial test for synonymous enrichment). The finding that synonymous variants are not enriched is important and properly interpreted. The linkage to prior GWAS (Figure 5—source data 3) and contribution of novel variants (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) are well-documented. The novelty claim (C100) is appropriately qualified as specific to P. falciparum growth associations.

result: Genotypic models of invasion were no more accurate than expected by chance (p≥0.3), though six of nine invasion receptors contained variants associated with growth. No principal components of population structure were significantly associated with P. falciparum growth rate, including PC1 (African ancestry). One PC was selected for 3D7 growth but was driven by a single East Asian donor.
evaluation: Claims C101-C105 report negative results for invasion prediction and population structure associations. The failure to predict invasion (C101) is consistent with the greater experimental noise documented earlier. The lack of PC associations (C104) is important for interpreting ancestry results later. The identification of the East Asian outlier (C105, Figure 5—figure supplement 5) demonstrates appropriate quality control. These negative results are well-supported and important for the overall conclusions.

result: African ancestry did not predict P. falciparum resistance in non-carrier RBCs (except for positive association with Th.026.09 invasion, R²=0.13, p=0.004). Greater African ancestry predicted reduced fragility, reduced dehydration, and more overhydrated RBCs—traits that actually predict greater parasite susceptibility. Among 22 protective alleles, 50% were more common in Africans (not more than expected by chance, p=0.5), with the three largest FST variants all more common in Europeans. There is no evidence that African populations are enriched for non-pathogenic RBC polymorphisms or phenotypes associated with impaired P. falciparum growth in vitro.
evaluation: Claims C106-C114 present a surprising and important finding that challenges assumptions about malaria selection on polygenic RBC variation. The analyses are rigorous, using OLS regression for phenotype-ancestry associations (Figure 6F-H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and FST calculations from gnomAD for allele frequency differences (Figure 6E). The binomial test for allele frequency enrichment (C111) is appropriate. The conclusion (C114) is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence and appropriately qualified as specific to non-pathogenic variation and in vitro growth.

result: The study demonstrates that widespread, normal variation in RBC hydration and deformability traits are associated with P. falciparum fitness in non-carrier RBCs, with a threefold range of parasite replication rates that overlaps with RBCs carrying protective variants. These protective phenotypes in non-carriers are also present in carriers to a stronger degree and are consistent with experimental manipulations (chemical/genetic dehydration) and rare variants (Dantu) that reduce parasite growth. This is the first demonstration that common, healthy phenotypic variation in RBC traits contributes meaningfully to P. falciparum growth.
evaluation: Claims C115-C122 synthesize the main findings in the context of prior work. The citations to prior studies (C115-C121) are appropriate and support the biological plausibility of the findings. The claim of novelty (C122) is justified—while prior work showed effects of disease alleles and experimental manipulations, this is the first systematic study of common variation in healthy RBCs. The integration of phenotypic and genetic data strengthens the conclusions.

result: The broad distribution of RBC phenotypes in humans is shaped by a large number of common alleles (consistent with polygenic models), with different combinations potentially underlying the variation observed in non-carriers. Some RBC phenotypes are also shaped by environmental variation (diet, time of day). Genetic variation in a small number of RBC proteins outperformed phenotypic variation in linear models, implying the existence of protective RBC phenotypes not measured or not measured with sufficient accuracy (e.g., proteomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic traits).
evaluation: Claims C123-C127 discuss the genetic architecture of RBC traits with appropriate citations to GWAS studies (C123) and environmental factors (C125). The inference about unmeasured phenotypes (C127) is reasonable given that genetic models outperformed phenotypic models. However, this could also reflect measurement error in phenotypes or the integrative nature of genetic effects. The speculation about specific unmeasured traits is appropriately qualified.

result: The study's candidate gene approach, focusing on 23 malaria-related genes, enabled discovery of associations with modest sample size by testing fewer hypotheses. However, genetic linkage complicates identification of exact functional polymorphisms—about half of associated variants occur in linkage blocks with other GWAS-associated SNPs. The evidence most strongly supports that 13 specific RBC genes are enriched for polymorphisms impacting P. falciparum growth. Future studies with many more than 68 non-carriers will be required to discover additional associations in unknown genes, non-genic regulatory variation, and smaller-effect alleles.
evaluation: Claims C128-C135 discuss methodological considerations and limitations. The justification for the candidate gene approach (C131) is sound and appropriately cited. The acknowledgment of linkage issues (C133-C134) is important and honest. The conclusion about 13 genes (C135) is appropriately conservative given linkage. The statement about future sample size needs (C132) is realistic. These claims demonstrate appropriate scientific caution and understanding of the study's limitations.

result: Associations for parasite growth were stronger than for invasion, likely due to batch effects, missing invasion data in 10 non-carriers, and the fact that growth includes a re-invasion event. The two strains (3D7 and Th.026.09) display large differences in absolute growth rate, possibly due to drug resistance alleles and differential lab adaptation. African ancestry predicted higher invasion only for Th.026.09, possibly indicating strain adaptation to African RBCs. Despite differences, normalized fitness values were significantly correlated between strains, and several phenotypes and genotypes replicated across strains, suggesting findings may be generalizable across divergent P. falciparum strains.
evaluation: Claims C136-C144 discuss strain-specific effects and generalizability. The explanations for weaker invasion associations (C137-C138) are plausible and supported by the data. The speculation about strain adaptation (C140-C141) is appropriately qualified with 'possibly' and 'might indicate.' The evidence for generalizability (C142-C143) is supported by the strain correlation data (Figure 2C, R²=0.69). The cautious conclusion (C144) appropriately acknowledges the need for testing more strains.

result: The lack of enrichment for protective alleles in African populations could be explained by: (1) insufficient time for frequency increases since P. falciparum expansion 5,000-10,000 years ago; (2) variants not substantially impacting severe malaria outcome; (3) pleiotropic effects subject to other selective pressures; or (4) adaptation too local to detect with coarse-grain sampling. Overall, the data suggest few RBC alleles remain to be discovered that are both particularly common in Africa and have large effects on P. falciparum proliferation in RBCs. It may be inaccurate to make assumptions about RBC susceptibility based on race or continental ancestry.
evaluation: Claims C145-C151 discuss possible explanations for the surprising lack of African enrichment. The four explanations (C146-C149) are all plausible and appropriately speculative. The citation to a similar finding from a large GWAS (C145) strengthens the conclusion. The overall inference (C150) is appropriately qualified ('few...remain') and specific to common, large-effect alleles. The broader conclusion about race/ancestry (C151) is well-supported by the data and important for clinical and research practice. This is a thoughtful discussion of unexpected results.

result: The study demonstrates that substantial phenotypic and genetic diversity in healthy human RBCs impacts malaria parasite replication. This result reminds us that >90% of total genetic variation among humans occurs within populations rather than across them, and the majority of common genetic variation is shared among all human populations. Whether or not this diversity is shaped by malaria selection, better understanding of how P. falciparum biology is impacted by natural RBC variation could help lead to new therapies for malaria.
evaluation: Claims C152-C155 provide concluding statements with appropriate citations to foundational population genetics work (Lewontin 1972, Rosenberg 2011, Biddanda et al. 2020). The main conclusion (C154) is well-supported by the entire body of work. The speculation about therapeutic applications (C155) is appropriately qualified with 'could help' and represents a reasonable long-term goal. These claims effectively contextualize the findings within broader population genetics principles.

result: The study's main findings are: (1) over one-third of healthy donors carried alleles for G6PD deficiency or hemoglobinopathies with characteristic RBC phenotypes; (2) among non-carriers, variation in RBC hydration, membrane deformability, and volume was strongly associated with P. falciparum growth rate; (3) common genetic variants in PIEZO1, SPTA1/SPTB, and invasion receptors were associated with parasite growth; (4) little or negative evidence for divergent selection on non-pathogenic RBC variation between Africans and Europeans. These findings suggest a model in which globally widespread variation in a moderate number of genes and phenotypes modulates P. falciparum fitness in RBCs.
evaluation: Claims C156-C160 summarize the main findings of the study. Each summary statement is well-supported by the detailed results presented earlier. The proposed model (C160) appropriately synthesizes the findings and is consistent with the evidence. This is an accurate and balanced summary of the study's contributions.
